items.title: Cooling efficacy of trees across cities is determined by background climate, urban morphology, and tree trait
items.summary: Abstract Urban planners and other stakeholders often view trees as the ultimate panacea for mitigating urban heat stress; however, their cooling efficacy varies globally and is influenced by three primary factors: tree traits, urban morphology, and climate conditions. This study analyzes 182 studies on the cooling effects of urban trees across 17 climates in 110 global cities or regions. Tree implementation reduces peak monthly temperatures to below 26 °C in 83% of the cities. In tropical, temperate, and continental climates, a mixed-use of deciduous and evergreen trees in open urban morphology provides approximately 0.5 °C more cooling than a single species approach. Existing evidence is based on process-based growth and ecosystem-service models, on water-balance studies of urban green spaces and irrigation, and on single-city monitoring campaigns, while multi-city in-situ observations under a consistent methodology are missing. items.title: Urban Heat Islands: Causes, Effects, and Mitigation Strategies
items.summary: An increasing environmental hazard linked to the world's cities' fast industrialization and urbanization is urban heat islands, or UHIs. This phenomena happens when temperatures in urban regions are noticeably higher than those in rural areas, mostly as a result of human activity, altered land surfaces, and heat-retaining materials like concrete and asphalt. UHIs worsen health risks, increase energy use, and degrade air quality, especially for disadvantaged groups. The fundamental causes of UHIs are examined in this research, including plant loss, urban geometry, surface features, and anthropogenic heat emissions. The study also explores the diverse impacts that UHIs have on biodiversity, public health, air and water quality, and energy demand. items.summary: Trees play a key role in mitigating urban heat by cooling the local environment. This study evaluated the extent to which street trees can reduce sub-canopy air temperature relative to ambient conditions (ΔT), and how ΔT relates to tree traits and microclimatic variables. Air temperature under the canopies of 10 species was recorded within residential areas in Western Sydney, Australia, during summer 2019–2020. items.summary: Forest restoration has never been higher on policymakers' agendas. items.title: Cool cities: The value of urban trees
items.summary: This paper estimates the value of urban trees and shows their ability to moderate temperatures during heatwaves and reduce energy consumption.The empirical strategy exploits an ecological catastrophe-the Emerald Ash Borer infestation in Toronto-to isolate exogenous variation in neighborhood tree canopy changes and finds that a single tree adds 0.45% to property prices within a postal code; the hardest-hit areas lost 7 percentage points in tree canopy cover, resulting in a 7% property price decline.Trees significantly cool urban areas and save energy, but their total amenity value surpasses the value of these ecosystem services, highlighting their costeffectiveness in combating urban heat island effects.
